g.text: Three shapes of data — and why batch is the special case
bounded · unbounded-as-batch (2 of 9 events misplaced) · unbounded-as-streaming
BOUNDED — ALL NINE EVENTS, AS A FINITE FILE
read to the end → sort by event time → one answer per window → job exits
every window, final and correct — because the input ended
There is no watermark here and no lateness, because "has everything arrived?" has a free answer: the file ended.
Note that id 7 lands in its CORRECT window. Batch over a finished input is not approximately right — it is right.
Step 1/4 — bounded data: it ends, so completeness is free
Start here, because it is the case where none of this book's problems exist. The input ends, so you can sort by event time, and every window is
final. id 7's 230s of skew is harmless: it was in the file before the job started. Everything difficult later comes from removing exactly one
Three shapes of data — and why batch is the special case
bounded · unbounded-as-batch (2 of 9 events misplaced) · unbounded-as-streaming
UNBOUNDED-AS-BATCH — sliced into 120s chunks of PROCESSING time
2 of the 9 events are in a chunk that is not their event-time window: ids 6 and 7.
From INSIDE a chunk there is no way to notice. Each chunk is internally consistent, finishes cleanly, and reports a wrong number.
Step 2/4 — unbounded data as batch: slice by the WRONG clock
This is the pattern most "streaming" systems actually are: a batch job on a timer. It works, it is simple, and 2 of 9 events land in the wrong
bucket — id 6 by 50s and id 7 by 230s. The chunk boundary is a fact about the pipeline's clock, and it is being used to answer a question about
Three shapes of data — and why batch is the special case
bounded · unbounded-as-batch (2 of 9 events misplaced) · unbounded-as-streaming
UNBOUNDED-AS-STREAMING — each window closes when the watermark crosses its end
windows are 120s of EVENT time; closing is a PROCESSING-time moment
Window [12:00, 12:02) closes after event id 4 — and id 7 arrives 3 events later, so it is LATE by construction.
The last window never closes at all: no event ever pushes the watermark past its end. "Unbounded" includes the state you are left holding.
Step 3/4 — unbounded data as streaming: close on the watermark
Streaming keeps the event-time windows (so the buckets are right) and makes CLOSING a separate, processing-time decision. That split is what
batch-on-a-timer collapses. The price is visible on both ends of this table: the first window closes before id 7 shows up, and the last one is
still open with 8 in it and nothing to trigger it.
Three shapes of data — and why batch is the special case
bounded · unbounded-as-batch (2 of 9 events misplaced) · unbounded-as-streaming
the grouping key is the only thing that differs
group by event-time window · every window final at end of input (event 9)
group by PROCESSING-time chunk · 2 of 9 events misplaced
group by event-time window · each closes when the watermark crosses
Rows 1 and 3 use the SAME grouping key and get the SAME buckets. They differ only in WHEN they declare a window done.
Row 2 is the odd one out — and not because it is batch. It is wrong because it keyed on the arrival clock.
So: bounded is unbounded data whose watermark jumps to "everything" at the end of input. One model covers both.
Step 4/4 — batch is the special case, not the other way round
The usual framing — "batch for history, streaming for live" — makes these sound like two systems. They are one. A bounded input is an unbounded
one whose watermark reaches infinity at EOF, which closes every window at once. Keep that and you can write a pipeline once; the shape of the
input decides when it speaks, not what it computes.
